paper_title: When to Rethink: Learning Multi-Perspective Self-Verification for Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain prone to generating plausible but incorrect answers. Self-verification offers a practical way to improve answer reliability without relying on external judges, but existing methods typically depend on a single verification criterion or fixed prompt, resulting in incomplete and unstable reliability estimates. We first systematically analyze how verifier capability and prompt design affect verification performance. Our findings show that stronger verifiers provide more reliable judgments, while verification performance is highly sensitive to prompt choice, with no single prompt consistently dominating across tasks. Guided by these findings, we propose \texttt{MOTIVE}, a \textbf{M}ulti-View Self-Verificati\textbf{O}n wi\textbf{T}h Rel\textbf{I}ability-Guided Selecti\textbf{VE} Rethinking framework for reliable multimodal reasoning. \texttt{MOTIVE} evaluates each candidate answer from complementary verification perspectives and learns a correctness-aligned reliability score through correctness-grounded multi-view verification learning. During inference, this score governs an accept-or-rethink decision, allowing reliable answers to be returned directly while uncertain ones trigger history-guided rethinking. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal benchmarks and VLM backbones demonstrate that \texttt{MOTIVE} consistently outperforms strong self-verification and self-correction baselines. Further results show that reliable verification improves accept-or-rethink decisions and reduces unnecessary reasoning turns, enabling more reliable and efficient self-verification without an external judge.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multimodal understanding, enabling strong performance across diverse visual question answering and reasoning tasks (Dai et al., 2023; Dong and Crisan, 2025; Bordes et al., 2024). However, despite their impressive capabilities, VLMs remain prone to generating plausible but incorrect answers due to visual ambiguity and reasoning errors (Huang et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b). Therefore, enabling VLMs to assess the reliability of their own predictions is crucial for building more trustworthy multimodal systems (Ghosh et al., 2024). To improve the reliability of VLMs, recent studies have explored self-verification mechanisms that enable models to examine and assess their own generated answers (Zhang et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2024a; Cheng et al., 2024). Compared with external verification approaches that require additional models or computational 1 MOTIVE When to Rethink resources, self-verification provides more efficient way to evaluate predictions within the same multimodal model (Campbell et al., 2024; Anis et al., 2025). However, existing self-verification methods typically rely on single verification criterion or fixed checking procedure (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), which may fail to capture diverse types of errors in multimodal reasoning. As result, how to obtain more reliable and comprehensive verification signals remains an open challenge. To better understand the factors affecting self-verification reliability, we conduct preliminary analyses on verification capability and prompt design in Section 2. Our studies reveal two important observations. ❶ Verification effectiveness depends on verifier capability. Stronger verifiers provide more reliable assessments by better understanding visual evidence, question semantics, and answer consistency, indicating that verification quality is closely related to the reasoning ability of the verifier. ❷ Verification performance is sensitive to verification prompt design. Different verification prompts exhibit complementary strengths, while no single prompt consistently performs best across different multimodal tasks. These findings suggest that reliable self-verification benefits from diverse verification perspectives and the effective aggregation of complementary signals. Guided by these findings, we introduce MOTIVE (Multi-View Self-VerificatiOn wiTh RelIability-Guided SelectiVE Rethinking), self-verification framework for reliable multimodal reasoning. MOTIVE evaluates each candidate answer through complementary verification views and aggregates their outputs into unified reliability score. Correctness-grounded verification learning supervises both view-specific judgments and the aggregated score using automatically derived candidate-correctness labels. During inference, the learned score governs an accept-or-rethink decision: reliable answers are returned directly, whereas uncertain ones trigger history-guided rethinking. This design improves verification decisions within the same backbone VLM without requiring an external judge. Our efforts are unfolded with the following four thrusts: (Preliminary Analysis) We systematically investigate verification capability and prompt design, showing that stronger verifiers improve answer reliability, while self-verification remains highly prompt-sensitive and no single prompt consistently dominates across tasks. (Algorithm) Guided by these findings, we propose MOTIVE, multi-view self-verification framework that uses correctness-grounded verification supervision to support reliability-guided accept-or-rethink decisions without an external judge. (Experiments) Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and three VLM backbones demonstrate that MOTIVE consistently outperforms strong self-verification and self-correction baselines. (Extra Findings) We further find that reliable verification enables earlier stopping with fewer unnecessary rethinking turns, while the best individual verification view varies across datasets and backbones, confirming their task-dependent complementarity.

sections.title: 2 Preliminary Analysis
sections.content: Before presenting our method, we analyze how verification capability and prompt design affect the answer reliability of VLMs in visual question answering.

sections.title: 2.1 Verification Capability
sections.content: We first examine whether explicit verification improves the answer reliability of VLMs. Given multimodal query, the baseline directly uses Qwen2.5-VL-3B or Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025a) to generate the final answer. In the verification setting, the backbone first produces an initial answer, which is evaluated together with the image and question by an external judge constrained to output YES or NO. YES verdict 2 MOTIVE When to Rethink retains the answer, whereas NO triggers rethinking and regeneration. We use InternVL3-2B, 8B, 14B, and 38B (Zhu et al., 2025) as judges and evaluate on VQA (Antol et al., 2015), ScienceQA (Lu et al., 2022), and TableVQA (Kim et al., 2024). The main observations are summarized below. Figure 1: Effect of Verification Judge Capability. Accuracy on three benchmarks using Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B backbones and InternVL3 judges of different scales. Dashed lines denote performance without verification. ① Verification Enhances Final Answer Reliability. As shown in Figure 1, introducing verification consistently improves final-answer performance over direct answering across different backbones and benchmarks. This indicates that the initial responses of VLMs are not always sufficiently reliable. By determining whether an answer should be accepted or regenerated, verification provides an opportunity to correct unreliable responses without modifying or fine-tuning the backbone model. ② Stronger Judges Improve Verification Effectiveness. We further observe that larger InternVL3 judges generally achieve better final performance across different Qwen backbones and multimodal benchmarks. This indicates that verification effectiveness depends on the judges multimodal reasoning capability, particularly its ability to assess the consistency among visual evidence, question semantics, and the generated answer. External verification improves VLM reliability but requires an auxiliary judge and introduces additional computational cost, motivating self-verification within the backbone VLM. This provides more practical way to assess answer reliability without requiring an additional model during use.

sections.title: 2.2 Verification Prompt Design
sections.content: We next examine how prompt design affects self-verification performance. Since external judges introduce additional computational cost, we use the same backbone VLM for both answer generation and verification. Based on representative self-correction and self-verification protocols (He et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2023; Dhuliawala et al., 2024), we compare two prompt families: five predefined Direct Verification Prompts (DVP1DVP-5), provided in Appendix B.1, which assess the initial answer from complementary perspectives, and Generated Verification Questions (GVQ-1GVQ-3), which generate and answer one, two, or three auxiliary verification questions, respectively, before producing final YES/NO verdict. YES verdict retains the initial answer, whereas NO triggers rethinking and regeneration. We conduct the analysis using Qwen2.5-VL-3B on VQA, ScienceQA, and TableVQA, varying only the verification prompt. The main observations are summarized below. ① Self-Verification Is Highly Prompt-Sensitive. As shown in Table 1, changing only the verification prompt leads to clear performance variations under the same backbone, datasets, and verification protocol. This indicates that self-verification cannot be reliably elicited by an arbitrary checking instruction. Its effectiveness depends on whether the prompt provides clear criterion for assessing the initial answer, as different prompts may lead the same VLM to produce inconsistent verification decisions across multimodal tasks. 3 MOTIVE When to Rethink Table 1: Effect of Verification Prompt Design. Among DVP-1 to DVP-5, the best-performing prompt varies across benchmarks, showing that no single direct prompt provides universally reliable verification view. Although all DVP prompts follow the same direct YES/NO verification format, their effects are task-dependent, suggesting that each prompt captures only part of the evidence needed for reliable answer checking. Relying on one fixed prompt may therefore overfit the verification behavior to specific benchmark or question type. This motivates the use of complementary direct prompts to obtain more reliable and informative verification signals across tasks. ③ Generated Verification Questions Introduce Instability. GVQ-style prompts are generally less stable than direct verification prompts, and their performance further decreases as more auxiliary questions are generated. Although GVQ makes the verification process more explicit, these intermediate questions are generated by the same VLM that produced the initial answer. As result, they may inherit the models original uncertainty, shift attention away from the original query, or introduce additional reasoning errors before the final verdict. This suggests that increasing the number of self-generated verification steps does not necessarily strengthen verification, but can amplify intermediate uncertainty and error propagation. These findings indicate that the central challenge of self-verification is not adding more reasoning steps, but establishing reliable criterion for judging whether the initial answer should be trusted. single direct prompt provides incomplete and prompt-sensitive signals, while generated verification questions introduce uncertainty. This motivates multi-view self-verification framework that aggregates complementary signals and learns to distinguish reliable answers from unreliable ones.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Datasets. We conduct experiments on five visual question answering benchmarks: ReFocus (Fu et al., 2025), VQA (Antol et al., 2015), SLaKE (Liu et al., 2021), ScienceQA (Lu et al., 2022), and TableVQA (Kim et al., 2024). The selected benchmarks cover general image understanding, structured-image reasoning, medical VQA, scientific multimodal reasoning, and table-based visual question answering. Specifically, VQA evaluates general visual question answering over natural images; ReFocus focuses on structured visual inputs such as charts and tables; SLaKE targets medical VQA with radiology images; ScienceQA requires image-grounded scientific reasoning; and TableVQA tests fine-grained understanding of table images. We follow the official splits and evaluation protocols for all datasets. More dataset details are provided in Appendix A.1. Models and Baselines. We evaluate MOTIVE on three representative publicly available VLM backbones: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025a), and InternVL3-2B (Zhu et al., 2025). These models cover different parameter scales and model families, allowing us to evaluate whether MOTIVE consistently improves verification reliability across diverse vision-language backbones rather than being specific to particular model architecture. We compare MOTIVE with several groups of baselines. The first baseline is the vanilla VLM, which directly generates the final answer without self-verification. The second group includes prompt-level self-reasoning and self-verification methods, including Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2023), Self-Verification (Weng et al., 2023), and Chain-of-Verification (Dhuliawala et al., 2024). The third group includes recent multimodal self-improvement and self-correction methods, including ADPO (Qiu et al., 2026), R3V (Cheng et al., 2025), and LLaVA-SCo (Liu et al., 2025). For methods originally developed for language-only reasoning, we adapt their verification or correction prompts to the vision-language setting by conditioning on the same image-question input. All baselines are evaluated under the same datasets, answer-matching protocol, and decoding budget unless otherwise specified. 7 MOTIVE When to Rethink Implementation Details. For each backbone, all methods are evaluated using the same dataset splits and answer-matching protocol. We train MOTIVE with the AdamW optimizer using an initial learning rate of 1 106 and BF16 precision. During GRPO training, we use rollout group size of = 8 and sampling temperature of 1.0. We employ = 5 verification views and aggregate their reliability scores by arithmetic averaging. The acceptance threshold is set to τ = 0.5, the maximum number of candidate-answer turns is = 3, and the verification objective is weighted by λver = 0.1. We use official evaluation scripts when available; otherwise, multiple-choice and open-form answers are evaluated by exact option matching and normalized answer matching, respectively. Additional hyperparameters are provided in Appendix A.2. 4.1 Main Results Table 2 summarizes the main comparison across five VQA benchmarks on three VLM backbones. We observe that prompt-level methods such as Self-Consistency, Self-Verification, and CoVe improve over the vanilla VLM, but their gains remain limited, suggesting that prompt-only self-checking is not sufficient for reliable visual answer verification. Recent multimodal self-improvement methods, including ADPO, R3V, and LLaVA-SCo, provide stronger baselines, yet MOTIVE consistently achieves the best performance across different model scales and task domains. This consistent pattern indicates that the advantage of MOTIVE comes from modeling and aggregating complementary verification signals, rather than relying solely on sampling, reflection, or post-hoc correction. sections.title: 4.3 Effectiveness of Multi-View Verification
sections.content: To verify that the gains of MOTIVE arise from combining complementary verification views rather than from single strong prompt, we evaluate five single-view variants and the full model on five benchmarks with three VLM backbones. Each variant retains one verification view while all other settings remain unchanged. As shown in Table 4, the best single view changes across datasets and backbones, and no individual view is consistently superior. In contrast, MOTIVE achieves the highest and most stable overall accuracy, validating the necessity of multi-view verification.

sections.title: 4.4 Efficient Reasoning via Reliable Early Stopping
sections.content: To examine whether MOTIVE can avoid unnecessary rethinking, we compare its average reasoning turns with conventional Self-Verification under the same maximum budget of = 3. lower value indicates that the model can accept reliable answers earlier and requires fewer repeated revisions. As shown in Table 5, MOTIVE consistently reduces the average number of reasoning turns across all backbones and benchmarks. The reduction is more pronounced on challenging tasks such as VQA and SLaKE, where conventional Self-Verification is more likely to repeatedly reconsider uncertain answers, while smaller reductions are observed on ScienceQA, where reliable answers can already be identified relatively early. These results demonstrate that MOTIVE not only improves answer reliability but also enables more efficient reasoning through better early-stopping decisions.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Self-Verification in Multimodal Reasoning. Recent advances in multimodal reasoning have increasingly explored self-verification and self-correction mechanisms to improve the reliability of vision-language models (Ding et al., 2026). Rather than relying solely on single-pass prediction, these methods encourage 12 MOTIVE When to Rethink Figure 6: Effect of the calibration loss weight βcal. Accuracy (%) on five benchmarks under different values of βcal using Qwen2.5-VL-3B. models to re-examine their intermediate reasoning or final answers through reflection (Yan et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a), critique (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025b), verifier-guided assessment (Weng et al., 2023; Ding and Zhang, 2025; Wu et al., 2025a), or iterative correct (Gou et al., 2024; Manakul et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). Such designs have shown promise in reducing inconsistent predictions and improving performance on complex visual reasoning tasks (Qian et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2024), where errors often arise from weak visual grounding or unstable multi-step inference (Yin et al., 2024; Si et al., 2021). However, most existing approaches treat verification primarily as an inference-time strategy for refining final outputs (Luo et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a), instead of explicitly modeling the supervision carried by the verification process itself. As result, the fine-grained signals embedded in multi-turn self-verification, especially those associated with intermediate candidate answers, remain underexploited during training. Verifiable Supervision and Training Signals for VLMs. Beyond inference-time correction, another line of research seeks to improve reasoning models by turning verifiable outcomes into explicit training signals (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026b,a). In tasks where answer correctness can be automatically checked, prior work has explored reward-based learning (Bai et al., 2025b; Meng et al., 2025), process supervision (Zhang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026b; Han et al., 2026), and intermediate guidance to enhance model reliability without relying entirely on manual annotations (Guo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhan et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025). These methods demonstrate that verifiable feedback can serve as an effective and scalable supervision source for vision-language models, especially in settings that require structured reasoning and precise decision making (Chen and Song, 2025; Marsili and Gkioxari, 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). Nevertheless, existing approaches typically emphasize final-answer correctness (Wang et al., 2025b; Ong et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024), while paying less attention to the supervision value of intermediate verification trajectories. In particular, they seldom model the consistency between round-wise candidate answers and corresponding verification judgments, leaving multi-turn selfverification signals insufficiently exploited during training.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we investigated self-verification in vision-language models and showed that its effectiveness depends on verifier capability and prompt design, with no single verification prompt consistently dominating across tasks. Guided by these findings, we proposed MOTIVE, multi-view self-verification framework that aggregates complementary verification signals and learns correctness-aligned reliability through viewlevel and aggregate-level verification supervision. The resulting reliability score supports accept-or-rethink decisions, enabling uncertain answers to be selectively revised within the same backbone VLM without requiring an external judge. Experiments across five benchmarks and three VLM backbones demonstrate that MOTIVE improves final-answer performance, verification decision quality, and early stopping. 13 MOTIVE

sections.content: A.1 Additional Dataset Details ReFocus. ReFocus (Fu et al., 2025) evaluates structured-image understanding over visually complex tables and charts. The benchmark contains 2,219 questionanswer pairs collected from six subsets covering Wikipedia tables, synthetically rendered tables, table verification, scientific charts, and horizontal and vertical bar charts. Its questions require fine-grained information extraction, comparison, counting, aggregation, and multi-step reasoning over structured visual content. VQA. VQA (Antol et al., 2015) is large-scale open-ended visual question answering benchmark based primarily on natural images from Microsoft COCO. Its real-image portion contains approximately 204,000 images and 614,000 human-written questions covering object recognition, attributes, counting, spatial relationships, activities, and commonsense reasoning. Multiple human answers are collected for each question to account for linguistic variation and answer ambiguity. SLaKE. SLaKE (Liu et al., 2021) is bilingual medical VQA dataset containing 642 radiological images and 14,028 EnglishChinese questionanswer pairs. It includes CT, MRI, and X-ray images covering the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvic cavity. The questions examine imaging modality, anatomical structures, organ positions, abnormalities, and medical knowledge. We use the English-language questions in our experiments. ScienceQA. ScienceQA (Lu et al., 2022) contains 21,208 multiple-choice questions collected from elementaryand high-school science curricula, of which 10,332 are associated with image contexts. The questions span natural science, social science, and language science and may include scientific diagrams, natural images, textual contexts, candidate answers, lectures, and explanations. We use the image-based subset to evaluate multimodal scientific reasoning. TableVQA. TableVQA-Bench (Kim et al., 2024) contains 1,500 questionanswer pairs constructed from table images across multiple domains, including Wikipedia and financial documents. The tables exhibit diverse layouts, styles, fonts, borders, and cell structures. The benchmark evaluates visual cell recognition, rowcolumn alignment, comparison, aggregation, numerical calculation, and reasoning over structured table content. A.2 Additional Implementation Details All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA B200 GPUs. 1 The internal weights of the verification objective are set to βagg = 1.0 and βcal = 0.1, while the computation-aware reward coefficient is set to = 0.05. The verification loss weight is set to λver = 0.1. During inference, MOTIVE uses = 5 verification views, an acceptance threshold of τ = 0.5, and maximum of = 3 reasoning turns. For each verification view, the view-specific reliability estimate is given by the probability assigned to the YES output, and the final reliability score is obtained by averaging the estimates across all verification views. The computation-aware rollout reward is used to compute group-relative advantages in GRPO, while the auxiliary verification objective jointly supervises view-specific judgments and aggregated reliability scores. 1All experiments, data and model access, and processing activities were conducted by the University of Leicester. 21 MOTIVE

sections.title: B Prompt Details
sections.content: When to Rethink B.1 Direct Verification Prompt Templates In Section 2.2, we analyze different verification prompt designs and observe that no single direct verification prompt consistently dominates across all benchmarks. Based on this analysis, we adopt the five predefined Direct Verification Prompts (DVPs) as complementary verification views in MOTIVE, as described in Section 3. These prompts evaluate candidate answer from different perspectives, covering overall correctness, visual evidence support, backward evidence checking, global contextual consistency, and error discovery. Specifically, DVP-1 performs general correctness verification without additional constraints; DVP-2 focuses on whether the answer is directly grounded in observable image evidence; DVP-3 verifies whether the evidence required by the answer can be identified by reasoning back from the predicted conclusion; DVP-4 examines the consistency between the answer, the question context, and the overall visual scene; and DVP-5 adopts an error-seeking perspective to detect potential contradictions or mistakes in the candidate answer. Together, these complementary views provide diverse criteria for evaluating answer reliability. The complete DVP templates are summarized in Figure 7. Figure 7: Overview of the five Direct Verification Prompts (DVPs) used in MOTIVE. Each prompt evaluates the same candidate answer from different verification perspective and produces binary YES/NO judgment. B.2 Initial Answer Generation Prompt The initial candidate answer is generated using fixed prompt template, as shown in Fig. 8. This prompt is shared across all experiments to maintain consistent answer-generation protocol and ensure that the performance improvements mainly come from the subsequent verification process rather than prompt 22 MOTIVE When to Rethink variations at the initial stage. The template defines the image-question input format, the general answering requirements, and the expected output structure, allowing the VLM to produce standardized candidate answer before entering the verification procedure. In particular, the generated response serves as the initial hypothesis that is evaluated by the verification modules and may be further refined through the rethinking process when the reliability estimation indicates insufficient confidence. By fixing the initial generation prompt, all comparisons remain under the same inference setting, enabling fair evaluation of the proposed verification framework. Figure 8: Initial answer generation prompt. The prompt template used to generate the initial candidate answer for VLM inference. B.3 Rethinking Prompt Figure 9: Rethinking prompt. The prompt template used to trigger answer regeneration when the previous response is considered unreliable by the verification process. When the current answer is not accepted by the verification process, the model enters rethinking stage using the prompt template shown in Fig. 9. Different from the initial answer generation prompt, the rethinking prompt explicitly incorporates the previous response together with the original image, question, and initial prompt head, allowing the model to reconsider its earlier prediction under the same task context. The instruction verifier disagrees with your response. Think again. encourages the model to revise potentially 23 MOTIVE When to Rethink unreliable answers rather than simply repeating the previous output. This prompt provides simple and consistent mechanism for triggering answer refinement, enabling the proposed framework to selectively improve uncertain predictions while avoiding unnecessary regeneration for already reliable responses.

sections.title: C Additional Experiments
sections.content: C.1 Sensitivity Analysis of Acceptance Threshold We further investigate the effect of the acceptance threshold τ used in the accept-or-rethink decision. While lower threshold allows the model to terminate verification more easily, it may accept unreliable answers, whereas higher threshold encourages additional verification but may introduce unnecessary rethinking. As shown in Figure 10, the performance remains relatively stable across different threshold values, indicating that MOTIVE is not sensitive to specific manually selected threshold. The default setting of τ = 0.5 achieves the best performance across all five benchmarks, providing an effective balance between reliable answer acceptance and selective rethinking. These results demonstrate that the learned reliability score provides reliable decision signal for controlling the verification process. Figure 10: Effect of the acceptance threshold τ . Accuracy (%) on five benchmarks under different values of τ using Qwen2.5-VL-3B. C.2 Computation-Aware Reward Analysis We further analyze the effect of the computation-aware reward coefficient by varying its value while keeping all other training configurations unchanged. The coefficient penalizes unnecessary rethinking turns, encouraging the model to terminate verification once reliable answer is obtained. As shown in Fig. 11, increasing consistently reduces the number of rethinking turns across different benchmarks, while the final accuracy remains largely stable. Although larger penalties achieve stronger computation reduction, an excessive value (c = 0.10) may cause premature stopping and slightly degrade accuracy. The selected coefficient = 0.05 provides favorable trade-off between maintaining answer quality and avoiding redundant rethinking. C.3 Maximum Reasoning Turns Analysis We further analyze the effect of the maximum reasoning budget while keeping all other settings unchanged. As shown in Fig. 12, increasing the maximum number of reasoning turns from = 2 to = 3 consistently improves the performance across VQA, ScienceQA, and TableVQA, showing that one additional rethinking opportunity is beneficial for correcting uncertain answers. In contrast, further increasing the budget to = 4 or = 5 only yields marginal gains, indicating diminishing returns from additional reasoning turns. Therefore, we adopt = 3 as the default setting, since it captures most of the performance benefit while avoiding unnecessary extra computation. 24 MOTIVE When to Rethink Figure 11: Effect of computation-aware reward coefficient c. Accuracy (%) under different maximum reasoning budgets on three benchmarks using Qwen2.5-VL-3B. C.4 Sensitivity Analysis of Verification Views We further investigate how the number of verification views affects the performance of MOTIVE. Starting from the predefined verification view bank, we randomly sample views for verification while keeping all 25 MOTIVE When to Rethink other training and inference configurations unchanged. As shown in Table 8, using single verification view leads to inferior performance due to limited and potentially biased verification signals. Increasing the number of views from = 1 to = 3 consistently improves accuracy across all benchmarks, demonstrating the benefit of aggregating complementary verification perspectives. Further increasing the number of views to = 5 achieves the best overall performance, while the gain over = 3 becomes smaller, indicating diminishing returns from additional verification views. The model initially confuses the two plan sections and predicts 1.39%, for which the five verification views produce an aggregated reliability score of 0.27 < τ , triggering rethinking.
